title: Campos-Chaves v. Garland
lead: Three noncitizens received initial notices missing hearing dates and times, followed by notices specifying hearings they later missed. Their efforts to reopen removal orders required the Supreme Court to distinguish a valid initial notice from the notice needed to rescind an order entered in a person’s absence.

actors.name: Campos-Chaves
actors.role: El Salvador national whose reopening request failed in the Fifth Circuit.

actors.name: Singh
actors.role: Indian national whose favorable Ninth Circuit ruling also left an alternative argument open.

actors.name: Mendez-Colín
actors.role: Mexican national with a separate favorable Ninth Circuit notice ruling.

actors.name: Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
actors.role: Administrative appellate body reviewing the immigration judges’ decisions.

actors.name: Justice Jackson
actors.role: Dissenter joined by Sotomayor, Kagan, and Gorsuch.

proceedings: The Court affirmed the Fifth Circuit in Campos-Chaves, reversed the Ninth Circuit in Mendez-Colín, and vacated and remanded Singh because an exceptional-circumstances theory remained undecided. The initial-notice rescission theory failed where proper notice of the missed hearing was received.
limits: The ruling did not combine deficient documents into a compliant paragraph (1) notice or overrule Pereira and Niz-Chavez on initial notice and stop time. Other rescission grounds remained distinct, including Singh’s unresolved argument. The account reports the 2024 decision rather than later proceedings.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Campos-Chaves misses the hearing specified after his initial notice
sections.cue: How did his later reopening request reach the Fifth Circuit?
paragraphs: Campos-Chaves, an El Salvador national, entered without inspection near Laredo in 2005. Three days later, the Government served a notice to appear charging removability and identifying the immigration court, but leaving the hearing date and time to be set. A notice sent a few months later specified September 20, 2005, at 9 a.m.

He did not attend or explain the absence. The immigration judge found removability proved by the required evidence and ordered removal in absentia, meaning without his presence. Thirteen years later, he sought reopening based on Pereira, the Supreme Court decision concerning a notice lacking time and place, and the deficient initial document. The judge and Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) rejected that ground. The Fifth Circuit denied review because he did not dispute receiving the later hearing notice.

sections.title: Singh misses two scheduled hearings and obtains a different appellate result
paragraphs: Singh, an Indian national, entered by climbing a fence near Calexico in 2016. Weeks later he received a charging notice marking date and time TBD. Five days afterward, the Government sent a specific hearing notice to his supplied address.

In October 2018, the court sent another notice setting November 26 at 1 p.m. Singh did not attend, but the Government lacked his file, so the court reset proceedings for December 12 at 9 a.m. and sent notice. He missed that hearing and was ordered removed in absentia.

In April 2019 he requested rescission based on Pereira and the original notice. The immigration judge and BIA rejected it. The Ninth Circuit held that absence of a compliant single-document notice to appear permitted rescission. Rehearing en banc was denied over twelve judges’ dissent. That court had not reached Singh’s separate exceptional-circumstances argument.

sections.title: Mendez-Colín attends several hearings before missing the individual hearing
sections.cue: How did his long procedural history return to the initial defect?
paragraphs: Mendez-Colín, a Mexican national, attempted entry at San Luis in 2001 with two other noncitizens while falsely claiming United States citizenship. His initial notice named the court but left date and time unset. He attended the hearing fixed by a later notice and further hearings in 2002, receiving notices personally or through counsel.

After finding removability, the judge scheduled September 15, 2003, at 9 a.m. for Mendez-Colín’s intended cancellation application and notified counsel. Counsel sought withdrawal shortly beforehand because of lost client contact but appeared at the hearing. The judge allowed withdrawal while retaining counsel to serve any in absentia order, deemed relief claims abandoned, and ordered removal in Mendez-Colín’s absence.

Two reopening motions failed. The BIA treated the appeal from the second as withdrawn when Mendez-Colín was removed while it was pending. About fifteen years later, he sought reinstatement based on the deficient initial notice. The BIA refused, but the Ninth Circuit granted review in an unpublished decision alongside Singh.

sections.title: The consolidated cases ask which notice defeats this rescission ground
sections.cue: What requirements did the parties agree had not been met?
paragraphs: Section 1229(a)(1) required a notice to appear containing specified information, including hearing time and place and the consequences of nonappearance. Niz-Chavez required that information in one document. Paragraph (2) required written notice of a new time or place and nonappearance consequences when proceedings changed or were postponed.

The Government had to prove required notice and removability by clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence before an in absentia order. Rescission was available for exceptional circumstances raised within 180 days, government custody causing absence without the noncitizen’s fault, or nonreceipt of notice in accordance with paragraph (1) or (2). The consolidated dispute concerned the last ground, §1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii).

The Government conceded every initial notice was deficient but relied on later proper notice of the missed hearing. The noncitizens argued that lack of either kind independently allowed rescission and that a paragraph-(2) change required an earlier compliant paragraph-(1) notice.

sections.title: The majority reads either form as sufficient for the hearing actually missed
sections.cue: Why did it link rescission to the original order’s notice requirement?
paragraphs: Justice Alito wrote for Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Thomas, Kavanaugh, and Barrett. The ordinary disjunctive or allowed either form of notice to satisfy the condition. Nearby authorization for in absentia removal likewise referred to paragraph (1) or (2) and singular written notice. Requiring both for rescission would make an order validly entered on one notice vulnerable for absence of both.

The majority did not say any notice of any hearing was enough. The relevant notice concerned the missed hearing at which removal was ordered. A later scheduling notice superseded the earlier schedule. Thus receiving a compliant initial notice would not defeat rescission if the Government changed the date without informing the person. That hearing-specific approach matched the other grounds excusing absence for reasons not attributable to the noncitizen.

The later notices here supplied the missed hearing’s time and consequences. A change could modify or replace TBD with a concrete date; Congress referred to any change. A new time could be newly supplied without replacing an earlier specific time, just as a new baby need not replace another. Adding Mendez-Colín’s individual hearing also changed his schedule.

sections.title: The earlier notice precedents remain in place on their own questions
sections.cue: Why did their language not control rescission here?
paragraphs: Pereira observed that paragraph (2) presupposed an earlier time-and-place notice, but addressed the stop-time rule for cancellation eligibility, not this paragraph’s meaning. The majority treated that observation as supplementary dictum. Niz-Chavez’s statement that paragraph (2) permitted changing an inconvenient selected time remained true without excluding other uses.

The Government still had to issue a proper notice to appear containing charges and other information necessary to present a case. A recipient of a later hearing notice nevertheless had to attend and could raise initial defects there, allowing rescheduling to cure prejudice. This rescission provision did not authorize indefinite challenges to defects that could have been raised at a hearing the recipient did not attend. Neither initial-notice nor stop-time holdings were overruled.

sections.title: Jackson views the initial notice as indispensable and later notice as supplementary
sections.cue: Why did the dissent reject the majority’s sequence?
paragraphs: Justice Jackson dissented with Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Gorsuch. Paragraph (1)’s contents were mandatory, and many never appeared in a later scheduling notice. Pereira and Niz-Chavez established that an incomplete initial notice did not become compliant through later backfilling. Focusing only on the missed hearing severed the statutory sequence.

A change notice resembled a construction change order, modifying selected terms of an existing instruction rather than replacing the whole. Change, postponement, and new time presupposed an already scheduled hearing. Any covered kinds of changes, not absence of the initial schedule. The word or accounted for situations where an additional notice would or would not be needed; it did not make the narrower conditional notice an equivalent substitute. Even an either-notice test would fail here because neither type was valid.

Jackson also resisted dismissing the earlier opinions’ statutory reasoning as dictum. Their treatment of the same provisions deserved respect. Her notes assumed the rescission question presented while questioning whether inadequate notice also defeated the initial order under the Government’s proof burden.

sections.title: The dissent sees a statutory burden shifted from government to the recipient
sections.cue: What historical and practical concerns supported its view?
paragraphs: Jackson traced notice rules through the 1952 Act, mandatory in absentia procedures introduced in 1990, and the 1996 scheme. Congress paired efficient removal with safeguards and incentives for both sides to comply. The prospect of reopening many orders resulted from governmental systemic noncompliance, not a reason to change that balance.

She warned that the majority supplied no adequate boundary for notices missing counsel information or even charges, which hearing notices did not reproduce. Requiring unfamiliar noncitizens to appear merely to protest the Government’s defect shifted Congress’s burden. She would permit rescission requests under these circumstances while reserving whether relief was automatic or discretionary.

sections.title: Three judgments receive different dispositions
sections.cue: What remained for Singh on remand?
paragraphs: On June 14, 2024, the Court decided the consolidated cases 5–4. It affirmed the Fifth Circuit’s judgment against Campos-Chaves and reversed the Ninth Circuit’s judgment for Mendez-Colín. It vacated and remanded Singh because his distinct exceptional-circumstances ground under §1229a(b)(5)(C)(i) remained unaddressed. The Supreme Court did not decide that alternative.

A proper later notice of the missed hearing defeated this particular notice-based rescission theory. The holding did not turn separate deficient documents into a compliant single-document notice to appear or change the stop-time rules.
